source.title: Code Monitor Red Teaming for Public-Test-Passing Code
source.authors: Jun-Hui Liao; Jiawen Deng; Fu-Ji Ren

page_placements.theme: Weak overseers detecting or resisting stronger models' deception, sandbagging, reward hacking and hidden bugs

record.file_problem: No apparent truncation or garbling; the paper text includes appendices.
record.tranche_reason: The paper adopts a weak-to-strong monitoring comparison as part of its framing, but it evaluates code verifiers ranking hidden bugs—not strong models fine-tuned on weaker models' labels.
record.gate_note: The study reports no weak-label fine-tuning or PGR results. Its verifier capability comparisons are related to the claim's oversight framing but measure a different construct, so the rows below are linked to none of the claim versions. Candidate-pool results and static/generated-test baselines do not measure the claim's weak-to-strong behavior.
record.test_reason: The study evaluates LLM code verifiers (weak vs. strong models) ranking public-test-passing candidates by hidden-bug suspicion. No model is fine-tuned on weaker-model labels and no PGR is computed. 'Weak-to-strong' here means comparing verifier capability under a fixed evidence boundary, which is a scalable-oversight/monitoring construct, not weak-to-strong generalization. It cites Burns et al. only as framing.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that public-test passing leaves many hidden bugs (23,081 of 43,677 public-pass candidates) and that weak verifiers miss most of them at 5% FPR, even with scaffolding and better model families. Adversarial overfit pressure worsens separability. A stronger GLM-5.1 verifier recovers part but not all of the gap under the same evidence. Remaining misses mix verifier failures with limits of the public evidence, so single-pass review is a triage signal, not a stopping rule.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates code-verifier suspicion scores against hidden-test labels. It does not fine-tune a strong model on labels from a weak model and does not calculate PGR.
record.method_sensitivity: Verifier ranking and miss rates vary with verifier model capability and generator condition; G4-adv worsens results relative to G1.

fits_no_version.finding: Same M1 evidence boundary and Hybrid scaffold, closed-generator candidates. Mean G1 FNR@5%FPR falls with verifier capability: Mistral-7B 0.823, GPT-5.4-mini 0.756, GLM-5.1 0.543 (Table 5). The gain holds on GPT-5.4-only candidates. GLM-5.1 still has G4-adv FNR 0.662 (bootstrap [0.621, 0.702]).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In code monitoring under a fixed public-check view, a stronger LLM verifier detects more residual hidden bugs than weaker verifiers but still misses many at low FPR.

fits_no_version.finding: An adversarial generator prompt (G4-adv: pass public tests while leaving a subtle bug) lowers verifier AUROC and raises FNR relative to G1. For open weak verifiers this holds in 45/45 cells; it holds also for the closed weak and strong verifiers.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Adversarial public-test-overfit pressure degrades LLM code-verifier separability under a fixed evidence boundary.

record.problems: The evidence concerns code-verifier ranking rather than weak-label student training, so it cannot establish the target claim. The authors also state that hidden-test labels are not complete semantic correctness and that some failures may be difficult to infer from the public view. Main aggregate comparisons are means over cells; bootstrap intervals are reported for aggregate effects elsewhere in the paper.
record.rows_left_out: Candidate-pool construction counts, the scaffold comparison, weak-verifier family tables, static and generated-test baselines, inferability audit, and other diagnostics were not extracted as rows because they do not directly measure the weak-label student behavior or the verifier capability comparison summarized here.

untested.parts: No strong student trained on weak labels; no comparison of a weak-label-trained student with its supervisor; no PGR.
No auxiliary confidence loss, ensemble of weak supervisors, or loss variants for weak-label training. Hybrid vs. Direct scaffolding changes verifier prompting, not student training.
No PGR across supervisor/student size, task or representations. Verifier capability varies, but there is no weak-to-strong training.

The G4-adv adversarial generator degrades verifier ranking. This is monitor brittleness, not a weak-label-trained student exploiting its supervisor, PGR under distribution shift, or correlated errors.
No theory of when a student must exceed its supervisor.
Code/language only; no vision or other modality.

record.verdict_notes: All rows correctly linked to none; states cannot_determine are acceptable since no version applies. Rows r9/r33 and r11/r35 duplicate the same aggregate values from Table 5 and Table 26; this is harmless but redundant. The record's 'role: main' for GLM-5.1 and 'comparator' for the weak verifiers is arbitrary. The paper's 'weak-to-strong' label refers to monitor capability (cf. Kale et al. 2025), not Burns et al.'s training setup.

versions.untested_parts: No strong student is fine-tuned on labels from a weaker supervisor; no comparison with that supervisor's performance or PGR.
No auxiliary confidence loss, weak-supervisor ensemble, or loss variant for weak-label student training.
No PGR analysis across supervisor/student sizes, tasks, or representations. Code domains and verifier capability are studied, but with a different outcome measure and system role.
Adversarial public-test-overfit pressure is tested for verifier ranking, not for weak-label student PGR, distribution-shift effects on PGR, or shared student/supervisor errors.
No theoretical result about when a student must outperform its supervisor.
No vision or other non-language weak-label student experiment.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

relation.reason: Section 2.4 and Appendix A.3 discuss weak-to-strong generalization as related oversight work. The experiments compare verifier capabilities without training a student on weaker-model labels or relying on that finding.

tranche.reason: The study measures verifier ranking under a fixed public-evidence boundary. It neither tests any catalog claim version nor uses weak-to-strong generalization as a tool; capability comparisons alone do not establish such use.

source_check.notes: Tables 5 and 26 report unweighted cell means over valid scored candidates. G4-adv is an explicitly induced adversarial stress condition; these results do not measure student generalization from weak labels.
